solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Anger 3 moderated (8)

blocks.note: temper = anger, as in 'lose your temper'
3 down is EDITOR, and ED is its standard short form

annotation.surface: Someone's anger has been toned down.
annotation.walkthrough: The number points to another answer: 3 down is EDITOR, which you then shorten to its everyday abbreviation ED.
annotation.definitionFit: Tempered means moderated, as in justice tempered with mercy.

entries.clue: Prince of Wales and son bringing one to portrait painter (4)

blocks.note: Prince Hal, Shakespeare's Prince of Wales who becomes Henry V

annotation.surface: A royal and his son travel together to sit for a portrait.
annotation.walkthrough: Prince Hal is the young Henry V of Shakespeare's Henry IV plays; putting HAL and S together brings you to the painter.
annotation.definitionFit: Frans Hals was the Dutch master of portraits such as The Laughing Cavalier.

entries.clue: Newspaper chief travelled up to cover it (6)

indicators.note: in a down clue, 'up' reads the word from bottom to top
EDOR is laid over IT, holding it inside

blocks.note: rode = travelled, on a horse or bus

annotation.surface: An editor-in-chief heads upstairs to hush up a story.
annotation.walkthrough: RODE turned upside down is ED…OR, and IT fills the gap.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain job title: the one who runs the paper and decides what goes in it is its editor.

entries.clue: Entire triangle at sea (8)

indicators.note: at sea = confused, so the letters are jumbled

annotation.surface: A whole triangle out on the ocean, perhaps a navigator's.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole clue is only three words, so the definition and the eight-letter fodder sit side by side.
annotation.definitionFit: Integral can mean whole or complete, as in an integral set.

entries.clue: Unnerve some coming over in old banger (10)

indicators.note: in a down clue, coming over turns the word upside down

blocks.note: to rattle someone is to unnerve them
part = some, then turned over to TRAP

annotation.surface: Riding in a clapped-out car is enough to shake anyone's nerves.
annotation.walkthrough: A banger is British slang for a battered old car; a rattletrap is one that shakes as it goes.
annotation.definitionFit: A rattletrap is a rickety old vehicle, just what a Briton calls an old banger.

entries.clue: Last in science, failing to pass (6)

blocks.note: a lapse is a failing, a slip

indicators.note: take the final letter of the next word

annotation.surface: A student who comes bottom in science and doesn't get through the exam.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Failing to pass' reads as exam talk; in fact the words split, 'failing' giving LAPSE and 'to pass' the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: Time is said to elapse when it passes.

entries.clue: Called for action about guy, duke, … (8)

indicators.note: DEED goes around the other pieces

annotation.surface: Someone calling on a man and a duke to act, running on into 9 across.
annotation.walkthrough: The ellipsis links this clue to 9 across so the two read as one sentence; each has its own answer.
annotation.definitionFit: To call for something is to demand it.

entries.clue: Leave suddenly, as banks of 15 affected (6)

indicators.note: the banks are the outside edges, so keep the first and last letters

blocks.note: 15 across is DANUBE; its outer letters are D and E

annotation.surface: Someone flees as floods on the Danube's banks strike.
annotation.walkthrough: 15 across is the river DANUBE, which makes 'banks' a neat way to ask for its two outside letters.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: striking camp and slipping away overnight is the picture behind the word.

entries.clue: … nobleman dividing New York almost (6)

indicators.note: EARL splits NY in two by going into it

annotation.surface: Continuing 7 across: an aristocrat is splitting New York.
annotation.walkthrough: The ellipsis joins this to 7 across as one sentence, but the wordplay here is self-contained.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: 'nearly there' and 'almost there' say the same thing.

entries.clue: Ring up about second musical work (4)

indicators.note: about = turned around, so UP becomes PU

annotation.surface: Someone phones about a second piece of music.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Ring up' reads as one phrase, to telephone; the clue wants the words apart, ring as O and up as UP.
annotation.definitionFit: Latin for 'work', used for composers' catalogue numbers such as Beethoven's Op. 27.

entries.clue: Watch a pet unravelling ribbon (6,4)

indicators.note: A PET comes apart and is rearranged

blocks.note: ticker is slang for a watch

annotation.surface: Keep an eye on a pet as it unwinds a ribbon.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Watch' looks like a verb, as in keep an eye on; it is the noun, a ticker.
annotation.definitionFit: Ticker tape is the paper ribbon on which old telegraph machines printed share prices.

entries.clue: Shopkeeper sounds more repulsive (6)

indicators.note: the answer is what 'more repulsive' sounds like

annotation.surface: A shopkeeper's voice is getting ever more unpleasant.
annotation.walkthrough: GROSSER and GROCER are said the same way.
annotation.definitionFit: A grocer is a shopkeeper who sells food.

entries.clue: Like onion rings? Agree with Little Richard, reportedly (10)

indicators.note: the answer is what the words sound like when spoken

blocks.note: consent = agree; Rick is a short, little, form of Richard

annotation.surface: A rock-and-roll fan nods along to Little Richard, with a side of onion rings.
annotation.walkthrough: Little Richard looks like the singer; here it is just a small Richard, RICK. The question mark flags that onion rings are one example of concentric rings.
annotation.definitionFit: The rings of an onion share a centre, which is what concentric means.

entries.clue: Carmen’s friend in car (8)

blocks.note: Mercédès is one of Carmen's gypsy friends in Bizet's opera

annotation.surface: Carmen's pal riding along in a car.
annotation.walkthrough: Carmen here is Bizet's opera heroine, whose friends Frasquita and Mercédès read her fortune in the cards.
annotation.definitionFit: Mercedes is both the operatic friend and the car brand.

entries.clue: Departs a centre on English river (6)

blocks.note: the nub is the centre or crux of something

annotation.surface: Someone leaves a centre by the river in England.
annotation.walkthrough: 'English river' looks like one phrase asking for the Thames or Avon; English gives only E, and the river is the Danube.
annotation.definitionFit: The Danube is the great river of central Europe.

entries.clue: Duo hired band (8)

blocks.note: a brace is a pair, as of pheasants
let = hired out, as a flat is let

annotation.surface: A pair of musicians taken on as a group.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface wants band to mean musicians; it is a band worn on the wrist.
annotation.definitionFit: A bracelet is a band worn round the wrist.

entries.clue: Clergyman in vicious circle (6)

indicators.note: a vicious circle is spun out of shape, so its letters are rearranged

annotation.surface: A priest caught in a vicious circle.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Vicious circle' is a stock phrase, which hides that 'vicious' is doing the work of mixing CIRCLE.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: any priest, vicar or minister counts.

entries.clue: Native American protagonist living mostly under cover, initially (8)

indicators.note: drop the last letter of KEEP
take the first letter of 'cover'
in a down clue, the HERO and KEE sit below C

blocks.note: the hero is the protagonist of a story
your keep is your living, as in earn your keep; lose the P

annotation.surface: A Native American hero lying low, living mostly under cover.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Living' is the noun, as in earning your keep, not the verb.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by class: one of the peoples of the south-eastern United States, so a member is a Native American.

entries.clue: Fresh in tavern, always (6)

indicators.note: the answer sits inside the words that follow

annotation.surface: The beer is always fresh in the pub.
annotation.walkthrough: The comma between tavern and always is ignored; the letters run across it.
annotation.definitionFit: Vernal means of the spring, and so fresh and youthful.

entries.clue: Produce dope, Ecstasy, and speed (8)

blocks.note: gen is British slang for information, like dope

annotation.surface: A drug dealer's list: making dope, ecstasy and speed.
annotation.walkthrough: Every word looks like a drug, but dope here means information, which Britons call gen, and speed is just rate.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, as when a power station produces electricity.

entries.clue: Satisfying? Fairly (6)

blocks.note: an adjective for what meets the need, sufficient
an adverb meaning moderately, placed after the adjective it softens

annotation.surface: A question and a shrug: was it satisfying? Fairly.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark admits that 'satisfying' only loosely means enough.
annotation.definitionFit: Enough is what satisfies a need, and it also means fairly, as in 'good enough'.

entries.clue: Quietly he interrupts young relative (6)

indicators.note: to interrupt is to break into the middle of something, so P and HE go inside NEW

annotation.surface: A man quietly cuts in on his young relative.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Young relative' reads as one phrase for the definition, but young gives NEW and relative alone is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by class: a sibling's son is one kind of relative.

entries.clue: Iranian heading off mysteriously for a magical land (6)

indicators.note: drop the first letter of IRANIAN
the remaining letters are rearranged

annotation.surface: A Persian traveller mysteriously sets off for a magical land.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Heading off' reads as setting off; it tells you to take the head off IRANIAN.
annotation.definitionFit: Narnia is the magical land of C. S. Lewis's children's books.

entries.clue: Dalesman, perhaps making stupid error then about name (10)

indicators.note: something stupid is muddled and senseless, so ERROR THEN is scrambled
about = around, so the jumbled letters go around N

annotation.surface: A Yorkshireman makes a silly mistake about someone's name.
annotation.walkthrough: A Dalesman is someone from the Yorkshire Dales in northern England, so one example of a northerner, hence 'perhaps'.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example, flagged by 'perhaps': the Yorkshire Dales are in the north of England.

entries.clue: Device used in a casino in Oxford, say (4)

blocks.note: the box from which blackjack cards are dealt
an Oxford is a style of lace-up footwear, and 'say' marks it as an example

annotation.surface: A gambling gadget turns up in a casino in the university city of Oxford.
annotation.walkthrough: Oxford looks like the city; it is the style of lace-up shoe.
annotation.definitionFit: A shoe is both the card-dealing box in a casino and footwear such as an Oxford.

entries.clue: Troublesome situation ineffectual types raised (4)

indicators.note: in a down clue, raising a word reads it bottom to top

blocks.note: a wet is a feeble, ineffectual person, British slang

annotation.surface: Feeble people have caused a tricky situation.
annotation.walkthrough: In British slang a wet is a weak, ineffectual person; WETS read upwards give STEW.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: someone 'in a stew' is in a state of worry over a tricky situation.

entries.clue: Fuel left out for fire (6)

indicators.note: the L is taken out of LIGNITE

blocks.note: lignite is brown coal, a fuel
l = left; this is the letter removed

annotation.surface: Fuel set aside to light a fire.
annotation.walkthrough: Fire here is the verb, to set alight.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, with fire as the verb: to fire a kiln is to light it.

entries.clue: I hang around and look ‘with it’ before start of rally (8)

annotation.definitionNote: the definition is the loiterer speaking: 'I hang around' describes the person

indicators.note: take the first letter of 'rally'

blocks.note: lo = look, as in 'lo and behold'
the quoted words point to IT itself

annotation.surface: A hanger-on hovering at a rally, trying to look fashionable.
annotation.walkthrough: 'With it' reads as trendy; in the quotes it simply supplies the word IT.
annotation.definitionFit: A loiterer is someone who hangs around, and could say 'I hang around'.
